readerTitle: Why the shop with fewer kettles sells more of them
caseNote: 가상 사례 (주방용품 매장 두 곳, 사내 교육팀) + 실제 연구 (Iyengar & Lepper 잼 연구, 메타분석 2편)
insight: 선택지가 많을수록 좋은 것이 아니라, 고객이 '어느 것이 나에게 맞는지' 쉽게 알 수 있을 때 산다. 고칠 대상은 선택지 수보다 비교의 어려움이다.
misconception: 선택지를 늘리면 더 많은 고객의 취향을 맞추므로 판매는 늘 늘어난다.

sources.text: Iyengar, S. S., & Lepper, M. R. (2000). When choice is demotivating: Can one desire too much of a good thing? Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 79(6), 995–1006.
Iyengar, S. S., Huberman, G., & Jiang, W. (2004). How much choice is too much? Contributions to 401(k) retirement plans. In Pension Design and Structure, Oxford University Press.
Scheibehenne, B., Greifeneder, R., & Todd, P. M. (2010). Can there ever be too many options? A meta-analytic review of choice overload. Journal of Consumer Research, 37(3), 409–425.
Chernev, A., Böckenholt, U., & Goodman, J. (2015). Choice overload: A conceptual review and meta-analysis. Journal of Consumer Psychology, 25(2), 333–358.

factChecks.note: 잼 연구 수치: 24종 진열 시 지나가던 손님의 약 60%, 6종 진열 시 약 40%가 시식대에 멈춤. 멈춘 손님 중 구매 비율은 24종 약 3%, 6종 약 30%. 원 논문 Study 1의 수치와 일치하는지 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요.
401(k) 연구는 펀드 수가 늘수록 가입률이 다소 낮아졌다고 보고합니다(펀드 10개 추가당 약 1.5~2%p 하락으로 알려짐). 카드에는 구체 수치 없이 일반적으로만 서술했습니다.
Scheibehenne 외(2010) 메타분석은 약 50개 실험을 종합해 평균 효과가 0에 가깝다고 보고했습니다. Chernev 외(2015)는 선택지 복잡성, 결정 과제의 어려움, 선호 불확실성, 결정 목표의 네 가지 조건에서 효과가 커진다고 정리했습니다. 카드 6·7의 서술이 두 논문과 맞는지 확인하세요.
주방용품 매장 두 곳과 사내 교육팀은 모두 설명용 가상 사례이며 수치(30종, 7종, 120개 강좌)도 가상입니다.

cards.title: Why the shop with fewer kettles sells more of them
body: Two kitchenware shops sit on the same street. Shop A stocks 30 kettles, every style and price. Shop B stocks 7.
Shop A has more of what any customer could want. Yet Shop B sells more kettles, and its customers leave happier.

image.label: Two shop shelves: one crowded with kettles, one with a few
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽 매장 선반에는 비슷비슷한 주전자 30개가 빽빽하게, 손님이 머리를 긁적이며 서 있음. 오른쪽 매장 선반에는 주전자 7개가 넉넉한 간격으로 놓여 있고, 손님이 하나를 집어 들고 웃음. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You run Shop A.
body: Plenty of people browse your kettle shelf. Many pick up two or three, compare the boxes, then say "I'll think about it" and leave.

options.text: Add more models so every customer finds an exact match
options.feedback: You cover more tastes, but you make the comparison even harder. The browsers who already can't decide now have more to weigh.

options.text: Cut to about 8 clearly different kettles and mark one as the staff pick
options.feedback: Each kettle now has an obvious reason to exist, and the pick gives unsure customers a safe place to land. You may lose a few people hunting for one exact model.
A discount gives people a reason to buy today, but it doesn't help them choose. You pay for the sale without fixing the hesitation.

cards.title: Shop B makes the choice easy, not small.
body: At Shop A, many kettles look alike. Customers compare wattage, colors and prices, worry they'll pick the wrong one, and put off the decision.
At Shop B, each kettle has one clear job: cheapest, fastest, quietest, best-looking, temperature control. A card says which one staff would buy.
Customers at Shop B don't do less thinking because there are fewer kettles. They do less thinking because **the differences are obvious**.

cards.title: Choice overload
body: **Choice overload** is when adding options makes people less likely to choose at all, or less happy with what they chose.
More options mean more comparing. They also raise the fear of regret: with 30 kettles, a better one is probably out there. Walking away feels safer than picking wrong.

image.label: A customer weighing many similar options versus a few distinct ones
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽: 비슷한 카드 30장이 사람 머리 위로 쏟아지고 "Compare… compare… later" 말풍선. 오른쪽: 서로 다른 아이콘이 붙은 카드 5장이 정돈되어 있고 "That one" 말풍선. 깔끔한 선과 두 가지 색만 사용.

cards.title: The jam table that started it.
body: In a 2000 study, researchers set up a tasting table in a grocery store. Some days it showed 24 jams, other days 6.

The big display drew more people in. The small one turned far more of them into buyers. Later work on workplace retirement plans found a similar pattern: plans with more funds had somewhat lower sign-up.

groups.label: Shoppers who stopped at the table
Of those who stopped, share who bought

cards.title: It's about how hard the choice is, not just the count.
body: A later review of many studies found overload is strongest when four things are true:
list: Options are **hard to compare** side by side
The customer **isn't sure** what they want
The customer has to **decide now**, not just browse
cards.callout: A regular who always orders the same coffee won't freeze in front of a long menu.
cards.softwareNote: The same pattern shows up on pricing pages with six plans and in sign-up flows that open with twenty templates. One highlighted plan or a "start here" template often does more than removing options.

cards.title: Fewer options isn't always better.
body: The effect is real in some settings and absent in others. A 2010 review of about 50 experiments found the average effect was close to zero. The jam study itself is debated, which a later lesson covers.
Variety also does a job: a wide range brings people through the door, and some customers come for one specific item. Cutting the range can lose them.
So the fix is often structure, not deletion. Group options, explain differences, and offer a recommended choice.

cards.title: Now it's a company's training team.
body: You lead the learning team at a 2,000-person company. Your online catalog grew from 40 courses to 120. Enrollment hasn't moved.
Managers say employees open the catalog, scroll, and don't know where to start. What do you do?

options.text: Add 60 more courses on the topics people requested
options.feedback: You meet every request on paper, but the scrolling problem gets worse. People who already can't start now have more to sort through.

options.text: Build three starter paths by role, each with one recommended first course, and keep the full catalog searchable
options.feedback: Unsure employees get an easy first step, and people who know what they want can still find it. It costs some design work and a few hard calls on what to recommend.

options.text: Delete everything except the 20 most popular courses
options.feedback: The catalog becomes easy to scan, but you lose the niche courses some teams truly need. You've fixed the count, not how people choose.

cards.title: People don't need fewer options. They need an easy way to choose.
body: When customers hesitate, look at how hard your options are to compare before adding or cutting any.
**Try it today:** pick the place where your customers choose most, a shelf, menu or plan page. Can a stranger tell in ten seconds how each option differs and which one you'd recommend?
